idiom_name: SQLAlchemy Session (unit of work + identity map + flush)
implementation_notes: SQLAlchemy's documentation names the pattern outright: the Session implements the unit of work pattern - objects added with session.add() participate in the flush, attributes are instrumented so mutations are recorded as they happen, and pending changes are flushed before queries and at commit, while the identity map guarantees one object per primary key. That replaces the classic role structure completely: no change lists and no manual flush ordering. Django is the other dominant Python stack and takes the boundary-only route: transaction.atomic (context manager or decorator, or ATOMIC_REQUESTS per view) provides the transaction and savepoints, but each model must be saved explicitly - the unit of work is the atomic block plus your save calls.
code_sketch:
with Session(engine) as session, session.begin():   # unit of work + transaction
    customer = session.get(Customer, cid)            # identity map hit
    customer.name = "new"                            # recorded, no SQL yet
    session.add(Audit(customer.id, "name"))          # queued INSERT
# flush before queries and at commit; rollback on exception

# Django - boundary plus explicit saves:
with transaction.atomic():
    customer.name = "new"; customer.save()
pitfalls: Autoflush issues pending writes before every query, producing statements you did not ask for and, with two sessions, deadlocks; autoflush=False is the escape hatch.
After commit all objects are expired by default, so touching an attribute triggers a fresh SELECT (expire_on_commit=False keeps them loaded).
A Session is not thread-safe and an AsyncSession is not safe to share between concurrent tasks; give each unit of work its own.
In Django the model fields are not reverted on rollback, so in-memory objects keep values the database never saw unless you refresh or discard them.

variants.name: Django transaction.atomic with explicit model saves
variants.implementation_notes: Django gives the boundary, not the tracking: atomic() opens a transaction (nested blocks become savepoints) and rolls back if an exception escapes, while each model instance must be saved explicitly. The unit of work is therefore the atomic block plus the list of objects you save in it - typically wrapped per request with ATOMIC_REQUESTS, and with transaction.on_commit() used for side effects that must not run on rollback. Choose it when the project is Django and the object graph is small enough that explicit saves stay readable.
variants.code_sketch:
with transaction.atomic():
    customer.name = "new"
    customer.save(update_fields=["name"])
    Audit.objects.create(customer_id=customer.id, field="name")
    transaction.on_commit(lambda: cache.delete(f"customer:{customer.id}"))
pitfalls: Catching IntegrityError inside the atomic block hides the failure from Django; the block must be exited with the exception, or an inner atomic block must wrap the risky statement.
Rollback does not restore in-memory attributes, and cache or global state updated inside the block is not reverted either - on_commit exists precisely for that.
ATOMIC_REQUESTS opens a transaction for every view, which adds overhead and holds locks for the whole request including rendering.
